You are correct and here's why: The top curly brace, being on its own line, is pointless. We already know we're starting a new block. We don't need to point it out twice. The if statement itself is declaration that a new block is starting (Only sadists use no curly brace on single line if statements, because those statements very often become more than single line later in development). However, there's no clear indication that the block has ended. When you stuff the closing curly brace with the else statement, it meshes multiple blocks into a single block when you're skimming. That single curly brace by itself at the end gives the clear indication that the block has ended, but a long else if can confuse because it starts to look like an indentation error instead of a declaration of a new block. The whole point of clean, readable code is that it's just that, which is why the opening of the block doesn't need to be on its own line, but the ending of the block does.

A fire breath could be avoided in the same way that if you quickly run over coals, or quickly put out a candle, you don't get burned. While true, it's a risk-reward system at its core where you take a risk, and if you are successful you are rewarded for it. The very foundation of the game. You can take the safe route and avoid an attack more round-about, but if you take the risk to avoid it more dangerously you gain from it when successful. The option of "normal" dodges is not gone, nor are they obsolete. There are many attacks that cannot be dodged even with the evasion armor skills. > Third, the game is mostly designed around putting a lot of weight behind concepts like positioning, distancing, timing, and aiming, and I love it for that. All of these things are supported with i-frames. If you position yourself incorrectly, you won't be able to dodge it. If you distance yourself improperly, your dodge will not go far enough (or go too far), and you will fail your dodge. If you dodge too early or too late, you will fail. If you do not angle your dodge correctly, you will fail.
